segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After these things I heard what sounded like the loud voice of a great crowd in heaven, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her prostitution, and he has avenged on her the blood of his slaves.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And a second time they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Hallelujah! Her smoke rises forever and ever.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God, who is seated on the throne, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Amen. Hallelujah!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And a voice came from the throne, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Praise our God, all you his slaves, and you who fear him, the small and the great.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard what sounded like the voice of a great crowd, like the sound of many waters and like the sound of mighty thunders, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Hallelujah! For the Lord, God the Almighty, has begun to reign.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Let us rejoice and be glad, and we will give him the glory, for the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and it was granted to her to clothe herself in fine linen, bright and pure.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the fine linen is the righteous acts of the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to me,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Write: ‘Blessed are those who are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to me,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “These are the true words of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I fell at his feet to worship him. But he said to me,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Don’t do that! I am a fellow slave with you and with your brothers and sisters who hold the testimony of Jesus. Worship God! For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw heaven opened, and look, a white horse! The one seated on it is called Faithful and True, and with justice he judges and makes war.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His eyes are a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems. He has a name written that no one knows except himself,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and his name is called the Logos of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the armies in heaven were following him on white horses, dressed in fine linen, white and pure.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From his mouth comes a sharp sword, so that with it he may strike the nations, and he himself will shepherd them with an iron rod; and he himself treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And on his robe and on his thigh he has a name written: King of kings and Lord of lords.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw an angel standing in the sun, and he cried out with a loud voice, saying to all the birds flying high overhead,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Come, gather for the great supper of God,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: so that you may eat the flesh of kings and the flesh of commanders and the flesh of the mighty and the flesh of horses and of those seated on them, and the flesh of all, both free and slave, both small and great.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies gathered to make war against the one seated on the horse and against his army.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the beast was seized, and with it the false prophet who had performed the signs in its presence, by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. The two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the rest were killed by the sword of the one seated on the horse, the sword that came out of his mouth, and all the birds gorged themselves on their flesh.

notes.note: A Hebrew liturgical shout meaning “Praise Yah” (a short form of God’s name), familiar to Greek-speaking Jews from the Psalms, where the Septuagint leaves it untranslated. Its only New Testament occurrences are the four in this chapter.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: “righteous/just” and “righteousness/justice.” Because God’s judging is in view, this translation uses “just” here and “justice” in verse 11, while the related noun in verse 8 is rendered “righteous acts.” Older versions have “righteous” and “in righteousness”; many modern versions also use “just” and “justice” in these verses.

The Greek noun is from the same root as the word for “prostitute” just before it, and the rendering keeps that echo. In Revelation the image draws on the prophets’ language for idolatry and corrupting alliances, not literal sexual conduct. Most versions have “fornication,” “immorality” or “adulteries.”

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and is the same word rendered “slave” in verse 18. Most versions soften it to “servants” when it describes God’s people. In the Septuagint it is also an honorific for those who belong wholly to God, such as Moses and the prophets.

The Greek verb is a past tense that can mark the start of a reign (“has become king”) or simply state the fact (“reigns”). Because the hymn celebrates God’s rule being openly established with Babylon’s fall, the first sense is chosen. Many versions have “reigns.”

notes.phrase: we will give him the glory
notes.traditional: let us give him the glory
notes.note: The Greek text followed here has a future tense, “we will give.” Many manuscripts instead have a form meaning “let us give,” matching the two verbs before it, and most English versions translate that reading. The difference in sense is slight.

“Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

The Greek can mean the testimony Jesus himself bore or the testimony others bear about Jesus; scholars are divided, and the rendering leaves both open. In the final sentence “spirit” could also be capitalized, making the point that witness to Jesus is what the Spirit inspires in prophecy. Some take that sentence as John’s comment and not the angel’s.

Nearly all translations have “the Word of God.” This translation keeps the Greek title “Logos” for the personal Word (as in John 1:1), because “the Word of God” now commonly means the Bible. Most scholars see the main background as the Hebrew Bible’s powerful “word of the Lord,” which “Word” reflects and “Logos” does not; here it fits the sword that comes from the rider’s mouth. In verse 9 the same Greek noun in its ordinary sense is rendered “words.”

Some manuscripts read “sprinkled with blood,” probably under the influence of Isaiah 63:3, where the one treading the winepress has his garments spattered. Interpreters disagree whether the blood is that of his enemies, as in Isaiah, or his own.

The Greek verb means to tend a flock and is often used figuratively of a king governing his people. The line echoes Psalm 2:9 in its Greek form, where the same verb appears. Most versions translate “rule”; “shepherd” keeps the image a Greek reader would have heard, though with an iron rod and in this context the sense is of harsh dominion, not gentle care.

notes.phrase: on his robe and on his thigh
notes.traditional: on his robe and on his thigh
notes.note: The Greek may mean two places, or the “and” may be explanatory: “on his robe, that is, at his thigh,” where the garment falls across the leg of a mounted rider. The rendering keeps the wording of the Greek and leaves the question open.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament both literally and for God’s people, and translators split between “slave” and “servant”; varying it hides that it is one word.
Recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation with literal and figurative senses, and English versions vary between “fornication,” “sexual immorality” and “prostitution.”
The Psalm 2:9 allusion recurs at Revelation 2:27 and 12:5, and the verb is used elsewhere of leaders and of Christ; “rule” versus “shepherd” should be decided once.
A key term in John and Revelation where “testimony” and “witness” compete, and the phrase “testimony of Jesus” recurs and should be rendered uniformly.
It pairs with ὀργή (“wrath”) in Revelation and Paul, and the two need stable, distinct English renderings across books.

warnings: Verse 9: λόγος is not rendered with a register form (Logos) and has no register-exception note.
